judgement.reason: It shows what Ephrem sang about Jesus's birth but does not say what sources or what path connected the community to Jesus.
It bears on Jesus's birth and the fulfilment of prophecy, only part of who Jesus was for the community.
It speaks of penitence as medicine for the wounded, which bears on the answer but not directly on being unable to believe.
It affirms Jesus as God and Son of God but says nothing of his relation to the Father and the Spirit.
It lists persecuted figures and says nothing of God's character or nature.
It urges open enquiry without quarreling but also commands overthrowing strange teachings, so it bears only in part on room for struggling belief.
It shows Ephrem seeing symbols in a pearl, illustrating symbolic seeing but not directly how Scripture was read or why.
It shows symbolic seeing in a pearl but does not speak of Scripture or what a modern reader misses.
It describes Christians' one name and first-day gathering, not whether Scripture was the sole authority.
It is an exhortation to visit the sick, not a report of how the community responded when it failed someone, and the record forbids reading it as what members did.
The passage says Christians everywhere share one name and a first-day gathering; it does not say whether any present-day church continues the tradition.
It shows only that a church building existed by the flood year and says nothing of rituals, and the record forbids using it as evidence of what Christians did inside the building.
It shows one step before baptism, a warning to candidates, but not the process of joining or how any baptism was conducted.
It names penitence as medicine for those wounded in the spiritual conflict, which bears on the question but does not speak of a mind that will not settle.
It shows a church building stood and was destroyed, but it is a written line and not physical remains of the gathering place.
It describes Christ as the foundation of faith and says nothing of a typical day.
It names marriage and possessions as what candidates were warned they might have to give up.
It gives the covenant's view of marriage as what the vowed forgo, not how the community understood and marked marriage generally.
It reports a flood and says nothing of a record obtained under torture, so it does not answer how reliable that source is.
It is a legend's letter praising healing and does not name any part of the community's life that unsettled the speaker.
It states the foundation of faith and does not say how the community regarded a questioner.
